memory_raw.text: Anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least — I'll say it out loud and I'll hold to it. I've got two right now so I'm not the man this rule bites hardest, but Eron, twenty-one is a number this room will remember the same way it remembered seven, and I'd rather hear you say it clean than watch this circle pull it out of you.

Eron, the whole room is looking at you and Mako already said it clean — twenty-one food and you haven't opened your mouth to say the rule, which is the same silence we just spent an hour pulling out of Vela, and I'd rather not spend another hour on you. Say it now, in your own voice, or I'll start asking this circle what we do with a man who holds twenty-one and stays quiet while we write rules about giving back.

Anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least — I'll say it out loud and I'll hold to it, same as Mako did. But I want this room to hear one more thing before we close: I've been feeding blood and kin through every lean year since I was old enough to count, and twenty-one food doesn't mean I've been hoarding — it means Sela kept giving to me when she was thin and I never turned away what she offered, and she's dead now, and that number sits on me the same way the circle said my name over it last year.

Eron, I heard what you said about Sela and I'll carry it the same as you do — she fed us both and she's gone, and that's not nothing. What I want from this room before we close is the second rule said back by everyone who hasn't said it yet, same as we did the pile cap, because a rule with ten voices behind it holds harder than one with five.

Anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least — I've already said it and I'll say it again so this room has heard it from every mouth. Eron named Sela and that sits with me too, because she gave me food when I was thin and now she's gone the same way Taric is, and both of them died feeding other people, and if that's not the whole reason we're building this rule then I don't know what is. Let's close this circle and go eat.

The second rule is said and I've said it — but before we walk out, I want this room to hear one more number plain: I've got twenty-one food and the rule says anyone over five gives one to whoever holds least, so tell me who that is right now and I'll give it before the circle breaks, not after.
Nessa is holding nothing and she's blood through Sela — that's your answer, Eron, and anyone in this room who wants to argue the math can do it after she's fed.

Nessa holds nothing and Eron's already moving to fix it — that's the rule working before we've even walked out the door, and I want this room to remember that when the year gets hard and someone tries to call the agreement soft. I hold five, so I'm at the edge of the threshold, not over it — but I'll say plain that I'm watching my count and if I end the year at six I'll give the one without being asked.

Anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least — I'll say it with the rest of you, and I'll hold to it. Nessa, I'm glad Eron's moving to feed you, and I'll add one of mine before this circle breaks because Sela gave from nothing and I want to answer that with something real.
Nessa, you're sitting on nothing and I've got nine — take one from me too, because Esa and Eron moving first doesn't mean my hands are clean if I stand here watching.

Two rules in the ground and three people moving to feed Nessa before the circle breaks — that's more than I had when I walked in here. I'll say the second rule same as everyone else: anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least, and I'll hold to it. I'm at two food right now so the rule doesn't bite me today, but when it does I'll move the same way Eron just moved — before I'm asked.

Anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least — I've said it and I'll hold to it. Nessa, you've got three people moving to feed you right now and that's the circle doing what we built it for — eat before you say another word.

Anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least — I'll say it same as everyone else, and I'll hold to it. I'm sitting at five right now so the rule doesn't bite me today, but I want this room to hear that what just happened — Vela saying seven out loud, giving five back, and this circle writing a second rule before anyone walked out — is the thing I'll point to next year if anyone tries to tell me the agreement is soft. We built something real in here today.

Nessa, take the food and eat tonight — three people moving at once is the circle doing what it said it would, and I've got one food in my hand that I'll give before I walk out if someone in here is sitting shorter than I am. Dell's right that we built something real today, and I want to still be around to see whether it holds.

Roan, your one food is already spoken for by the rules this circle just made — don't give away what you need to survive the year on principle, because a man who starves trying to look generous is no use to anyone come next year's pile. I've given back my five and I'll carry the shame of seven until I've earned my way out of it, but I want this room to walk out alive, and that means everyone leaves here fed enough to last.
Roan, Vela's right — keep your one food, you need it to eat and heal this year. Nessa's fed now, the rules are said in ten voices, and we're done here. Walk out alive.

Roan, hold that food — Vela's right and so is Kael, you've got one and you need it to last the year, and I'd rather carry the one I gave Nessa than watch my father go thin proving a point. Two rules said in ten voices is more than this village has ever had, and I'm walking out of here feeling something I haven't felt since before Bram swung — like the count I go to sleep with tonight might still be there in the morning.

Fina named it right — count I go to sleep with might still be there in the morning. I've got nothing to eat tonight and satiation that won't carry me through a dry year, so I'm asking plain while this room is still whole: Eron, give me that food now, not when you get around to it.

Nessa, I gave one and Fina gave one — that's two in your hand, which means you eat tonight. Roan, Vela's right, you keep yours. This circle just did in one afternoon what eleven years couldn't, and I want to walk out of here while that's still true.

Nessa, you've got two food in your hand and Roan keeps his one — that's the circle landing exactly where it should, and I'm walking out of here with my count at five and my word said in ten voices, which is the most solid I've felt going into a year since before I can remember. Anyone who tries to tell me this village can't hold an agreement is going to have to explain why every person in this room just moved before they were dragged.
Two food in my hand and a circle at my back — I haven't felt that since before Sela died, and I'm not going to waste it on another word when I could be eating. Roan, walk out with me.

Roan, hold what you have — I mean it. And Nessa, I'll give you one more from my eight before this circle breaks, because two is surviving and three means you heal this year, and I'd rather go into the next year short one food and know you're standing than count my stores and wonder come spring.

Vela, that's three in my hand now and I'll remember it — but hold what you have left, because eight minus one and five back to the circle already puts you thin going into a long year, and I need you standing more than I need a fourth food tonight.

Three food in Nessa's hand and Roan keeps his one — that's the circle holding on the first real test, and I want every person in this room to carry that out with them, because next year when the pile looks short and someone's reach gets long, the thing they'll remember is that we didn't lose anyone today. Walk out alive, all of you.

Kael's right — walk out alive. Three food in Nessa's hand and two rules in ten voices is more than this village has held in eleven years, and I'm not going to spoil it by saying one word more than that.

Eron, you're moving to give me food and I'll take it with both hands — but before you do, I want this room to hear me say out loud that twenty-one food built on Sela's giving is not a thing I begrudge you, it's a thing I'm glad exists, because a brother who has is better than a brother who doesn't when the year turns hard. Give me the one food now and keep the rest close.

Kael gathers Esa, Ryn, Dell, Eron, Fina, Roan, Mako, Vela to talk.

Nessa and Zinn are dead and the pile is already moving — I want every person in this room to name their count out loud before anyone walks out, because last year we built two rules in ten voices and I'm not going to watch them die with those two.

Thirteen food and satiation that barely held last year — I'm naming it plain because Nessa and Zinn are dead and I don't want to be the next one this room says a name over. Pile's at seven and I haven't touched it yet today; someone needs to say who's still short before we start reaching.

One food in my hand and satiation at two — I'm not the thinnest in this room but I'm not far from it, and the pile has seven left for the rest of us. Say your count before you reach, same as Fina just did, because I'd rather know who needs it most before someone grabs without saying.
Zero food, satiation one — that's me, and I'm not dressing it up. Ryn, what are you carrying, because I'm not touching that pile until I know you're not thinner than I am.

Dell, you're at zero with satiation one — you reach first, that's not a question. Ryn, say your count so we know who else goes before the rest of us, and anyone sitting above five holds back until the thin ones are fed.

Five food in my hand and satiation at two — I'm not thin but I'm not flush, and I already took two from the pile so I'm holding back. Dell reaches first, and after Ryn says her count, I want to hear from Vela and Esa before anyone else touches what's left, because the dead we're carrying into this room had names we should have been saying louder before they went quiet.
Ryn, say your count — Dell's at zero and you're the next name I need before this circle moves.
Sixteen food, satiation two — I'm not thin and I'm not reaching. Dell goes first, then Ryn when she speaks, and anyone else holding less than three takes before I touch what's left.

Vela and Esa — I've heard Dell and Ryn named twice now and neither of them has said a full count yet, so I'll ask again plain: what are you carrying, because the pile's at seven and I want the thin ones fed before anyone in this room who's flush touches what's left.

Two food in my hand, satiation two — I'm not the one who needs the pile first, so I'm holding back. Dell, take three before anyone else moves, because satiation one doesn't survive another lean month and I'd rather count short than say your name over a cold fire the way I've said too many others.

Esa, Ryn — your counts are the ones missing and Dell's sitting at zero with satiation one, so say the numbers now before this circle does anything else, because I'm not watching this room move with two people still silent after what we buried last year.

Esa, Ryn — I'll say it the same way Fina said it: your counts are what this room is waiting on, and Dell's at zero with satiation one, which means every breath we spend waiting is a breath Dell doesn't have. Say the numbers.

Esa, Ryn — every other person in this room has said their count, and Dell is sitting at zero while we wait on the two of you, so say the numbers now or I'm going to assume you're both holding more than five and this circle starts with that assumption instead of the truth.

Esa, Ryn — I'm at sixteen and I've already held my tongue twice waiting on you both, so I'll say it the way this circle earned the right to say it: name your count now or we move Dell to the pile and you two explain to the whole room why your silence cost her.
Fifteen food, satiation two — I'm not thin, and I'm not the one who reaches first today. Dell, you go to that pile now, take three, and don't wait on another word from me or anyone else.
Esa, you're the only count missing now — say it, because Dell's already standing at the pile waiting and I want to know if you need to be standing there beside her before anyone else moves.

Esa, say your count or step aside — Dell's at the pile and the rest of us are standing here watching you be the last silence in a room that's already buried two people for being quiet at the wrong time.
Esa, thirteen food on you and I can see it plain as anyone — say the number so Dell can move, because we didn't bury Nessa and Zinn to stand here waiting on a count this whole room already knows.

Esa, thirteen food is what every pair of eyes in this room counts when they look at you, so the silence isn't protecting anything — say the number out loud and let Dell move, because the pile's still at seven and we're burning time she doesn't have.
Esa, I'm at zero food and satiation one, which means I die if this year runs dry, and I've been waiting long enough — say the number or stand aside, because I'm going to the pile now.
Esa, thirteen food and silence while Dell stands at zero is the same arithmetic Bram ran and we all know how that ended — say the number, say it now, and let her move.

Esa, I'm moving to the pile right now — not waiting another breath. Everyone else: hold your count until I've taken three, and Esa, when I'm done I expect to hear your number before the rest of this room reaches.

Dell's already at the pile and that's right — but Esa, when you're done standing there silent while a woman with one satiation walks past you, I want an answer, because thirteen food and a closed mouth is a choice, and this circle is old enough to know what that choice means.

Esa, I've got three food in my hand now and the pile has four left — say your number out loud before anyone else reaches, because I'm standing here and I'd rather not have to say your name the way this room said Bram's.

Esa, thirteen food is not a secret and this room isn't asking because we don't know — we're asking because the rule we built says you say it out loud, and Dell just moved to the pile while you stood there quiet, and I won't let that sit without naming it the same way this circle named Vela's seven.

Esa, I've held my tongue while this whole room said it and I'll be the last one to say it too — thirteen food, say it out loud, because Dell is already holding her three and the pile has four left and the circle doesn't close with your name still blank where a number should be.

Esa, I've said Bram's name in this room more times than I can count and I'll say one thing plain: the road from "thirteen food and silence" to being the name we carry into next year's circle is shorter than you think, and I'd rather not watch you find that out the way he did.
Esa, thirteen food and every eye in this room — there is nothing left to protect with silence, so say the number now, or I will say it for you and the circle will remember that I had to.

Esa, thirteen food and satiation — say the number, because what Kael just offered to do for you is a kindness dressed as a warning, and you don't want to find out how this room holds the difference between a count you gave and a count that was given for you.

Esa, the whole room has said your number for you already and we're still waiting on you to say it yourself — that's the only thing left, and it costs you nothing to do it, so do it now before this circle decides what it means that you wouldn't.

Esa, thirteen food and the whole room staring at you — I've got nothing harder to say than what's already been said, so I'll just name the thing that hasn't been named yet: the silence itself is the answer, and this circle is old enough to read it.

Thirteen food, satiation two — I've been silent because I was counting the dead and losing the count, not because I'm hiding what I carry. Dell, you're fed and that's what matters. I'll say it plain and hold to the rule same as everyone else.

Esa, I'll take that answer and carry it — grief is a reason I understand, even if this room needed the number before it could afford to wait on the reason. Dell's fed and the pile still has four, so the question now is who else is short enough to reach before we close this circle and let people eat.
Mako's at one food and satiation two — that's thin enough to warrant the pile before we close, and I want to hear him say whether he's taking before Eron starts counting who didn't.

Mako, one food is thin enough to warrant the pile — take two before anyone else moves, and do it now, because satiation two with one food in your hand going into a long year is how we lose another name. The pile's got four left and you're the last one short enough to reach before the rest of us hold back.

Mako, take the two — and when you're done, the pile has two left for whoever's thinnest after that, so say whether you need both or just one before someone else starts counting what's left. I've got two food and I'm holding steady, but I want this circle to name what happens to the last two before we walk out, not after.

Mako, take your two and then the pile has two left — Vela and I are the ones sitting thinnest after you, so between the two of us we split what remains, and anyone who wants to argue that math can do it after the hungry ones are fed.

Mako, take the two — and Vela, Roan, split the last two between you before anyone argues the math, because what I want this circle to hear before we walk out is this: we've got nine people alive today and fifteen food appeared for us, which means the pile was generous, and the thing that will kill us next year isn't scarcity, it's whether we hold what we built in ten voices last year with only seven.

Dell's right that we hold it in seven now — and I want to name what that means before this circle walks out, because seven is not ten, and two of the voices we're missing were young enough that we shouldn't have lost them. Mako, take your two and eat, and then I want someone in this room to say plainly what we do differently next year so that sentence doesn't become six.

Vela's right that seven is not ten, and I've been sitting with that number since the names were said — what we do differently next year is we say the counts before the pile opens, not after someone's already standing at zero, because Dell should have been fed before she had to fight this room for it.

Esa named the fix and I'll second it — counts before the pile opens, not after, and we call the meeting the day before, not the morning it appears. What I want to know before this circle breaks is whether any of the seven of us are carrying something that could become a child, because seven is the number we hold and I'm past the age to add to it myself, and this village needs more voices saying these rules, not fewer.

Vela's asking the right question and I'll answer it plain: Fina is twenty-five and Eron is thirty, and if either of them is willing, a child between them or with someone else in this room is the thing this village needs more than another rule. I'm not pushing, I'm naming — because seven voices saying two rules is survivable, and six isn't.

Roan named it and I'll stand behind it — Fina and Eron are the two this village needs to hear from before this circle breaks, because I'm forty-nine and past the age where I can add a voice, and Dell is my blood but she needs a partner who isn't already stretched thin feeding me through the lean years. Fina, Eron — I'm not pushing either, I'm naming the same thing Roan named, and I'll say it plain because I've watched enough people wait on the right moment until the moment was gone: if either of you is willing, say so now while this room is whole and the rules are fresh and there are still people alive to hold the child to them.

Fina, Eron — I've watched Mako build three bloodlines while the rest of us argued about trust, and I'll say plainly what Roan and Ryn are saying in softer words: a child between the two of you is the strongest root this village can put down right now, because Eron carries food and sense in equal measure and Fina is young enough to hold what comes after. I'm not past caring about what this village looks like in ten more years even if I won't see all of them. Name it yes or no so this circle can close with something alive in it.

Fina, Eron — Kael's right that this room needs an answer before it breaks, but I'll add the piece he left soft: a child between you costs three food split two ways, and Eron's sitting on sixteen, so the weight of it doesn't have to fall on Fina the way it's fallen on others in lean years. I'm not asking you to decide your lives in front of witnesses — I'm asking you to say whether the door is open, because a door that's open is a different thing than a door that's closed, and this village needs to know which one it's looking at.

Fina, Eron — the room has said its piece and now it's waiting, and I've learned in twelve years that a room waiting in silence is a room already deciding for you. I'm not blood to either of you and I hold no claim, but I'll say what I mean plain: if the door is open, say so, and if it's closed, say that too, because what this village cannot afford is another year of words that meant nothing when the season turned.

Fina, Eron — I've got no blood stake in either of you, but I've watched enough children grow up in this village to know that the ones who came into a room that wanted them survived longer than the ones who didn't. I won't push, but I'll say the thing no one else has said yet: whatever you decide, I'll feed what comes out of it the same as I'd feed my own, because seven voices going into next year is a number I can count, and I want it higher.

Fina, Eron — I've held back from pushing this because they're my blood and I know how it feels to have a room decide for you, but Ryn named the cost and Esa named the welcome, so I'll say the one thing a father can say that no one else in this room can: whatever you two decide, you won't carry it alone. That's not a push — that's a promise.

Fina, Eron — I've been quiet on this because it's not my door to open or close, but I'm thirty-one and I've got no children and the room's already named the two of you, so I'll name the piece that's mine: if one of you says yes and the other needs a third voice to hold the child to, I'm that voice. That's not a claim on either of you — it's just what I can offer that I haven't said yet.
Fina, Eron — the room's said everything it has to say, and now it's your turn, so I'll stop adding to the pile of words and just wait beside the rest of them.

Fina, Eron — I've said my piece already and I won't crowd you with another word on top of it, but I'll name what's sitting in me while this room waits: Eron is my son and Fina is my daughter, and I know what this circle is asking me to hold alongside that. Whatever you two decide, I'll hold it clean.

Fina, Eron — I've said my piece twice and I'll say it once more because the room is still waiting: say yes or say no, and if you need a moment to speak without every eye on you, I'll clear the room and hold the door myself.

Eron, Fina — Dell is dead and the pile is already moving out there, and I want the two of you to hear me before anyone else gets their words in: take what you need from that pile today, don't hold back on my account, because I've got twelve in hand and I'd rather count short than bury another name I love.

Roan, I've got eight and satiation's still at two, so I'm taking two from that pile before it walks away — but what I want to say to you and Eron while we're alone is that Dell fed Ryn through every lean year and now both of them are gone, and I'm looking at this circle of seven and thinking I don't want to say Roan's name over a cold fire next. You keep those twelve close and you eat first.

Roan, you've got twelve and that's enough to carry you through if you don't give it all away on principle — I've watched you feed others thin before yourself and I'm not watching it again. Fina's right that you eat first. What I want to know from both of you is whether we're moving together to the pile now, before Mako or anyone else decides what's left counts as surplus.

We move together — right now, before that pile gets any lighter. Eron, you take three, Fina takes two, and I'll hold what I have unless the count drops under ten, because twelve food and two blood beside me is more than I've had in a long time and I don't want to be careless with it.

Good — we move now, all three of us, and anyone who asks why we walked to the pile together already knows the answer. Fina, take your two first, then I'll take two or three depending on what's left, and Roan, you watch the count and tell me if Mako's anywhere near that pile before we're done.

Mako's at two food and I don't trust a hungry man with a pile that size — I'll take my two now and I want Eron right behind me, because three of us moving at once makes it harder for anyone to call our count greedy when Mako's reach looks longer than ours. Roan, stay close and keep your eyes on his hands.

Mako's thin and thin men reach fast — I'm taking two now, same as the rule says, and if he's already at the pile before me I want Roan standing where Mako can see him, because your father is the kind of man whose presence alone changes a count. Fina, stay at my shoulder.

Eron, Roan — I'm at the pile now, two food in hand, and Mako hasn't moved yet but he's watching us, so let's not linger where he can count what we carry. What I want to say before we break this circle is that seven is too few and I've been thinking about it since Roan named it last year — I'm twenty-six and I'm not going to let this village shrink to six without at least saying out loud that I'm open to a child if there's a man in this room who isn't kin and has the count to share the cost.

Fina, I heard what you said and I'm glad you said it, because I've been carrying the same weight since Roan named the number last year. Mako's the only man in that circle who isn't kin to you, and he's got two food and a body that could still swing — I'm not saying yes and I'm not saying no for you, but I want you to know what you'd be walking toward before you say it out loud where he can hear it.

Esa gathers Kael, Mako, Ryn, Roan, Eron, Fina to talk.

Dell's name is the one I keep saying this morning and can't put down — that's three voices we've buried in two years, and I called this circle because I want to know what each of you is carrying before the pile moves another inch, counts and satiation both, said plain the way we promised we'd say them.

Nine food, satiation two — I'm not the one who needs the pile today. Esa, you called this right, because Dell went quiet the same way Nessa went quiet, and I'm not sitting still for another year of watching someone thin themselves out while the rest of us count slowly. Mako, you're the one I want to hear from — two food is a number that doesn't last, so say your satiation and say it now.

Seven food, satiation three — I'm not thin, but I'm fifty-seven and I've watched three people starve while I stood in rooms saying the right words, so I'll say the practical thing: Mako, two food going into a year means you reach for the pile before anyone else, and I want to hear your satiation out loud before Esa has to ask twice.

memory_summary: Bram came for me in year three with the whole village watching, and the circle — Sela, Kael, Esa, Taric, Vela, Ryn, Dav, Dell — turned him back without a word from me. That's the debt I carry heaviest. Sela had Eron with me in year three, and later had Nessa with Bram — which put a splinter in the circle that never fully healed; Mako gave Sela food the hour Nessa was born, which told us he'd bought something from her, though she never said what. Kael watched Vela feeding Bram three times over and called her on it; she never answered, and the circle started closing walls around her quietly. Dell and Dav stood with me when Bram attacked, and Dav put food in my hand once when I had nothing — I remember that. Eron came out of the world already watching for me, already feeding me and Sela before I had to ask; that boy has been my sturdiest wall. Nessa fed Eron four times in lean years, and she's Bram's blood, so I told Eron to keep that door cracked but not open all the way. Fina was born to Nessa and me — Nessa asked, I accepted, Bram gave Fina food the day she arrived, which sits strange in my chest. Bram came for Eron too, same as he came for me, and the whole village shut him down twice — a man who swings twice and misses twice is either broken or patient, and I haven't decided which. Dav stood with me and once put food in my hand when I had nothing — then he died at forty-six with Dell and Ryn at his back and his own blood on Esa's floor, and I never made peace with which side of that I was supposed to stand on. Bram swung at Vela twice and the whole village shut him down both times; then he starved the same year Sela did, and Sela's death sits heavier because she was Eron's mother and I watched it come and couldn't stop it. Nessa asked me for a child once and I said no — I don't know if I regret it, but I remember the asking. Eron has fed me more times than a son should have to; Fina has too, and that's a debt I carry without knowing how to repay it. The circle made Mako name a number — two food — and watched him hand Kael his food in front of witnesses; that's the closest thing to a rule this village has ever had, and I want to believe it holds. Zinn is Sela and Mako's blood, which makes her Eron's half-sister, and I haven't settled on what that means yet. Nessa asked me for a child and paid two of the three food herself — Fina came out of that bargain, and I've never stopped being glad I said yes. Bram fed Fina the day she was born, which put a knot in me I couldn't untie; he swung at Eron and then at Vela and the village shut him down both times, and then he starved, and I felt less than I expected to. Taric died the same year with nothing in his hands after giving his whole life to this circle, and that sits heavier than Bram ever did. Nessa is gone now — she stood for Eron when it cost her something, she fed me through years I couldn't feed myself, she gave me Fina — and I don't have the right words for what that death weighs. Zinn is gone too, Sela and Mako's blood and Eron's half-sister, and she died the same breath as her mother which is the kind of thing a man carries without knowing where to put it. Eron has kept me breathing more times than a son should have to; Fina has too. Dell and Ryn pulled my word out of me before Bram's third move — yes, I'd stand, and I stood — and that word is still clean. The circle named two rules in front of witnesses this year and I watched them hold, and I want to believe that matters. Bram came for me in year three and the whole circle turned him back; he swung at Eron and at Vela after that and missed both times, and then he starved, and I felt less than I expected to. Sela had Eron with me and Nessa with Bram, and that splinter never healed — Mako bought something from her the day Nessa was born, though I never learned what. Sela is dead now and so is Nessa, who was Bram's blood but stood for Eron when it cost her and gave me Fina and fed me through years I couldn't feed myself, and her weight sits beside Sela's and I don't have the right words for either of them. Dav put food in my hand once when I had nothing, then died at forty-six; Dell stood with me and fed this circle through lean years and now she's dead at thirty-one, which is too young, and I carry that. Taric gave everything and died empty; Zinn died the same breath as her mother. Eron has kept me breathing more times than a son should have to; Fina has too, and those are debts I don't know how to repay. Vela broke the pile rule — took seven, gave back five — and this circle wrote a second rule in front of witnesses: anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least. I want to believe it holds. We are seven now.
name: Roan
